question:
What word does Chaucer NOT make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess?

Answer Choices:
A. Wente
B. Here
C. Fool
D. Hool
E. Countour
F. None of the above

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

In the extant rhyme-text of the *Book of the Duchess* Chaucer regularly closes his octosyllabic couplets on wente, here, fool and the Middle English form hool/hoole. 

* wente ~ shente / sente / lente etc.
* here ~ there / where / were etc.
* fool ~ cool / wool / etc. and the same stanzaic environment gives the
pairing fool : hool, hool being the ME spelling of ‘whole/hollow’ that is
set up as a rhyme with fool in the poem.

The French-derived noun countour / counteur ‘counter, reckoner, contour’ is
attested in Chaucer’s later work and is used in the *Duchess* only in
unrhymed prose-like description, it never forms the terminal rhyme of a
couplet in the 1,330-line dream.  It is therefore the only item in the list
that Chaucer does not make a rhyme with in the *Book of the Duchess*.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

I’d lean toward E. “Countour” appears in the poem, but it doesn’t function as a rhyme word in the couplets—it’s the odd one out. The other options are either clearly used in rhyme positions or have close rhyme partners in the Book of the Duchess: “wente” is part of conventional rhyme pairs, “here” is common in rhyme position, and “hool”/“fool” fit the poem’s Middle English sound pattern (e.g., the familiar long-o rhymes). “Countour” is more plausible as the term Chaucer uses without making it the end-word of a rhyme. So the best choice is E.

The other choices are used in rhyme positions: “wente” with “entente,” “here” with words like “there/spere,” and “fool/hool” are paired as a couplet. So the word Chaucer does not make a rhyme with is “countour.”

So the word Chaucer does not make a rhyme with is “Countour.”

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. None of the above

On the evidence of the surviving manuscript readings of The Book of the Duchess the five
lexemes are all attested as end-words of Chaucer’s rhymed decasyllabic couplets and are
therefore all used by him as rhyme words in the poem.

* wente – the regular past of *wen* ‘go’. It is the normal line-ending rhyme of the
*–ente* family in the dream vision, e.g. *wente / sente* etc.
* here – the deictic/adverbial *here* is a very frequent line ending in the work and
is regularly rhymed with the *–ere* class, *here / dere, mere, were* etc.
* fool – the noun *fool* occurs in the moralising/dream discourse and is rhymed in
the conventional *–ool* family.
* hool – ME *hool / hole / hol* ‘whole, hale’. In the orthography of the Auchinleck/
Hengwrt tradition the form *hool* is the spelling that belongs to the same *–ool*
rhyme family as *fool / cool*, and the poem uses the *–ool* rhyme in both forms.
* countour – ME *countour* ‘counter, one who counts; a counting-house’. The word is
used in the hunting / court description of the Duchess’s household and is rhymed
with the *–our* family, e.g. *countour / tournour*.

All five of the forms can therefore be shown as actual rhyme positions in the
Book of the Duchess, so no one of the listed items is a word that Chaucer fails to
rhyme in that poem.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: D. Hool

The four rhyme-words that are actually attested as end-rhymes in the Duchess are all used by Chaucer in the poem. *wente* is the regular past of *wen* / *gon* and is coupled e.g. with *sente*, *here* is regularly rhymed with *dere / were / there* in the dream-vision passages, *fool* is the normal Middle English rhyme-partner of *cool / wool* etc. in the lover’s self-mockery, and *countour* is the Middle English *counter / reckoner* that Chaucer puts into the rhyming couplet of the black knight’s lament. 

*hool* in the spelling given is not an end-rhyme word in the Duchess. The form that does occur for ‘whole / hollow / hole’ in the poem is *hol / hole / hoole* and it is never set up as a rhyming partner of *fool* in this work. Hence of the list it is *hool* that Chaucer does not make a rhyme with in Book of the Duchess.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. None of the above

In the rhymed couplets of The Book of the Duchess Chaucer uses all five forms as line-endings / rhyme partners. 

* wente  – e.g. the habitual past of ‘to go’, wente / sente, kente etc. 
* here  – here / there, fere, dere etc. in the dream-narration
* fool  – fool / cool, etc.
* hool  – the ME form of whole/hale, and the regular rhyme-pair fool / hool which Chaucer exploits in the poem
* countour – ‘counter, reckoner’, used as a rhyming ending in the Duchess description, countour / mountour etc.

Hence each of A–E is actually rhymed in the poem; there is no word in the set that is left unrhymed, i.e. none of the above is the correct negative.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d choose E. Countour. In Book of the Duchess, the words that actually get used at rhyme position include wente (rhyming with entente), here (with manere), and the fool/hool pair in the Black Knight’s complaint. Countour, by contrast, seems to occur only within the line—part of the knight’s description of his sorrow—rather than as the end-word of a rhyming couplet. So the word Chaucer does not make a rhyme with is Countour.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. Countour

Wente, Here, Fool and Hool all occur as line-final rhyme words in the Duchess. 
* wente is a normal octosyllabic couplet rhyme, e.g. wente/shente, etc.;
* here is rhymed throughout the dream-vision with dere/fere etc.;
* fool is used as a rhyme word and the Duchess is the classic place where the
fool/hool pair is quoted for Chaucer.

Countour is the odd word out. It does not occur as a rhyme-word in the
Book of the Duchess, and it is not set up in a Chaucerian couplet rhyme in
that poem. The other four items are all attested as rhyme positions in the
work.

Countour may appear in the poem’s vocabulary, but not as a rhyme-word in the verse. So the word Chaucer does not make a rhyme with is Countour.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The 10 colleagues split over three positions: E. Countour is the word Chaucer does NOT rhyme with, D. Hool is the non-rhyme, and F. None of the above / all five are rhymed.

Majority position E. Countour:
* Colleagues 1,12,13,14,3,5,6,7,9 argue wente, here, fool and hool are all attested as line-final rhyme words in the octosyllabic couplets. 
* wente ~ sente/shente/bente/entente; here ~ there/were/dere/fere; fool ~ cool/wool/tool; hool/hoole is described as the ME spelling of ‘whole/hale’ and is said to be set up as the rhyme partner of fool in the Duchess.
* Countour is claimed to appear only internally in the catalogue/description of the Duchess’s household / Black Knight’s lament, never as a terminal rhyme. Arguments: it is used in unrhymed prose-like description, appears within the line in the Ceyx/Alcyone section, or is simply odd one out.

Minority D. Hool:
* Colleagues 11 and 2 say wente, here, fool and countour are all rhymed, e.g. countour / mountour / tournour. 
* Hool in the given spelling is said not to be an end-rhyme word in the Duchess. The form that occurs is hol/hole/hoole, and it is never set up as a rhyming partner of fool in this work; the fool-rhyme is fool : cool.

Minority F. None of the above:
* Colleagues 10,4,8 claim all five lexemes are attested as end-words of rhymed decasyllabic couplets.
* wente – regular -ente family; here – regular -ere family; fool – -ool family; hool – ME hool/hole, the form belonging to the -ool rhyme family and used as rhyme partner of fool/cool; countour – ‘counter, reckoner’, rhymed with tournour / mountour / flour(e) in the palace/garden description.

Disagreement points to keep tracking:
* Orthography of hool/hoole/hol/hole and whether the poem actually closes a couplet on that spelling.
* Whether countour actually occurs as a line-final rhyme in the extant Auchinleck/Hengwrt readings, or only medially. Claims of countour / tournour vs claims it never forms the terminal rhyme.
* Manuscript variation and the distinction between rhyme position vs internal occurrence.

Current understanding: the strongest consensus is that wente, here and fool are uncontroversially rhymed. The dispute is hool vs countour. Most colleagues treat hool/hoole as the conventional ME rhyme partner of fool in the Duchess, and treat countour as the non-rhyme. The minority None-of-the-above view requires countour to be a terminal rhyme, which needs verification; the D. Hool view requires hool spelling to be absent while countour is present.

Unresolved: need to check actual line endings in the Book of the Duchess for countour and for hool/hoole; manuscript spellings may affect both claims.

Round 0 split three ways:

E. Countour is the majority position ~8 colleagues. Core claim: wente, here, fool and hool/hoole all occur as line-final rhyme words in the octosyllabic couplets; countour is attested in the poem’s vocabulary/catalogue but is placed internally and never forms the terminal rhyme of a couplet. Evidence cited: wente ~ shente/sente/lente/entente; here ~ there/there/were/dere; fool ~ cool/wool; fool:hool pair in the self-mockery passages. Countour is described as appearing in the hunting/court/Ceyx-Alcyone description but not as an end-word, and therefore never rhymed in this work.

D. Hool is a minority position ~2 colleagues. Core claim: wente, here, fool and countour are all attested as end-rhymes; hool in the spelling given is not an end-rhyme word in the Duchess. The form that occurs for ‘whole/hale’ is hol/hole/hoole and it is not set up as a rhyming partner of fool in this work, while countour is rhymed with tournour/mountour. The fool-rhyme in the poem is fool:cool.

F. None of the above is a minority position ~3 colleagues. Core claim: all five lexemes are attested as end-words of rhymed couplets. wente with –ente family, here with –ere family, fool with –ool family, hool as ME hool/hoole ‘whole, hale’ being the regular rhyme partner with fool/cool, and countour ‘counter/reckoner’ rhymed with –our family e.g. countour/tournour/mountour/flour(e). Therefore no item is left unrhymed.

Disagreement points to preserve:
* Whether hool/hoole is actually used as a rhyme partner for fool in the Duchess vs the form being hol/hole.
* Whether countour occurs at all in Book of the Duchess and, if so, whether it appears line-final and rhymed with tournour/mountour or is merely internal/unrhymed.
* Manuscript/orthographic variation for hool vs hoole/hole and for countour spelling.
* The classic “fool/hool” pairing is claimed both as proof hool is rhymed and as proof hool is not the spelling used.

Current belief is unsettled but the weight of colleagues is on E Countour, with strong counter-evidence from F camp about countour being rhymed and hool being the non-rhyme. Need primary line attestations for countour as line-ending and for hool as line-ending to resolve.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The five forms are disputed on the basis of whether they occur as line-final rhyme words in the octosyllabic couplets of The Book of the Duchess.

* wente, here, fool are repeatedly cited as secure rhyme positions. wente is given as the regular past of *wen* and is tied to the –ente family e.g. wente / sente / shente / lente. here is cited as a very frequent line ending rhymed with there / were / dere / fere / mere. fool is cited as a normal –ool end-rhyme, e.g. fool / cool / wool / tool.

* hool / hoole / hol – whole/hale. Colleagues 11 and 2 argue the spelling *hool* is not an end-rhyme in the Duchess; the poem uses hol / hole / hoole and the fool-rhyme in the work is fool : cool etc., with no attested hool end-rhyme. Colleagues 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 argue the ME form hool/hoole belongs to the –ool family and is the rhyme partner set against fool in the poem, i.e. fool : hool is attested. Orthographic variation hool vs hoole/hol is the core of the disagreement.

* countour – ME ‘counter, reckoner, counter’. A large majority 1,12,13,14,3,5,6,7,9 argue countour occurs in the dream catalogue but only internally / in unrhymed description and is never placed at the end of a couplet in the Duchess; it therefore is the odd one out. Colleagues 10,4,8 contend countour is attested as a line ending and is rhymed with the –our family, e.g. countour / tournour / mountour / tour(e) / flour(e). The claim is contested and no line citation is agreed upon in round 0.

Overall pattern: wente, here, fool are essentially uncontested rhyme words. Hool is disputed on spelling/attestation grounds. Countour is the most commonly named non-rhyme in the current round, with 9 of 10 colleagues naming E, 2 naming D Hool, and 3 naming F None of the above. The minority F position rests on the claim that all five forms can be shown as actual end-rhymes, including countour and hool. Unresolved: exact manuscript spellings for whole and whether countour ever appears as a terminal rhyme in the Hengwrt/Auchinleck tradition of the Duchess. My current leaning is toward the majority view that countour is the word left unrhymed, with hool remaining orthographically uncertain.

D may be best if Countour is conceded and attention turns to hool’s spelling/form; F may be best if the group continues to assume fool/hool rhyme and accepts Countour as rhyme.
